policy.notes: Primary author-submitted research; peer review is not implied. cs.AI was retired: 282 entries a fetch of which only 11% were new work, 914 of 1516 corpus items, 4 published. cs.LG is near-disjoint from it (2 shared ids of 570) and is 39% new, so nothing was lost. This feed is still 290 entries a fetch and remains the single largest intake until announce_type filtering lands.

Chemistry, planetary science, geophysics, atmosphere and soft matter. Every feed here was retrieved end to end through resolve_item_text at 5.4k-13.6k words with sections classified, so all five can carry the Technical rung. physics.chem-ph is the only chemistry route that survived testing at all: ChemRxiv, Chemistry World, C&EN and ACS all refuse us. Together these five are ~72 entries a fetch, a quarter of what cs.AI alone cost.
Neuroscience preprints, ~4 entries a fetch. Retrieved end to end at 5458 words, arxiv_html scored 0.95, sections classified.

A capped cross-section of the aggregate mathematics feed. The live feed carried 409 submissions when added, so only the newest 30 enter each cycle. arXiv's HTML/PDF resolver is already proven; this adds mathematical volume without pretending that topical arXiv feeds are independent outlets.

Robotics preprints, capped at 30 of 59 live entries when added. Complements readable institutional and journal coverage with primary methods, but shares one publishing origin with every other arXiv feed in the coverage audit.

CC BY. The single best fix for the biology hole: one fetch spans neuroscience, cell biology, microbiology, immunology, developmental biology, genetics, structural and evolutionary biology. Retrieved twice through our own resolver at 7453 and 12993 words, article_html scored 0.87, 3/3 key roles present. Robots allows /articles/ at crawl-delay 10. CAVEAT ON content_type: eLife publishes Reviewed Preprints (public peer review, no accept/reject) alongside Versions of Record, so peer_reviewed here does not mean the same thing it means at Nature and the reader-facing label should say so. Feed carries no per-item image, only the eLife logo, and no DOI, so no OpenAlex enrichment fires; the DOI is mechanically 10.7554/eLife.<article id> if that is ever wanted.

CC BY, ~2 items a day. The DOI is in the feed link so every item reaches the resolver already identified. Fresh items retrieve as article_html at 11384 words; once PMC deposit catches up the same DOI resolves as pmc_jats at score 1.00 with figures and floats, which is the best input the ladder ever gets. Robots crawl-delay is 30s, at our cap, but 2 items a day makes that cheap. FEED IS MIXED: research sits alongside editorials and essays with no type marker in URL or DOI, so default_content_type is a default and not an assertion; the classifier has to settle type from the fetched page.

CC BY, ~0.8 items a day, and the replacement for medRxiv as the medicine source that actually yields text. Research articles resolve via oa_pdf at 9245 words, score 0.96, 3/3 key roles, with the licence recorded; OpenAlex hands us the PDF so journals.plos.org is never fetched and the 30s crawl delay is never paid. Roughly a third of the feed is Perspectives and Essays which retrieve thin (~1200 words) but are legitimate explainer and correction shapes. Same caveat as PLOS Biology: no type marker in URL or DOI.

Open-access research spanning physiological sensing, medical imaging, monitoring, diagnostics and health software. The rolling feed carries 30 current entries. Two of two representative papers resolved through the existing PLOS JATS route at 5,885 and 6,739 words with full structure. This fills the computational and instrumentation side of biomedical engineering, but is not treated as the whole field.

policy.notes: Broad biomedical engineering: biomaterials, biomechanics, tissue engineering, organs-on-chips, medical devices and bioprocessing. The current 20-entry feed contains 13 Original Research papers, one Brief Research Report, five Reviews and one Perspective. Publisher categories type the 14 research entries as peer reviewed; reviews and perspectives remain other rather than being passed off as primary results. Two of two tested entries resolved as full text at 13,940-15,772 words.

Broad open-access research across more than 200 subject areas, added as a measured cross-field source rather than a substitute for specialist coverage. The feed exposes 30 current entries and uses the already proven PLOS JATS resolver. Its field yield will be audited after generation; a capped broad feed is useful only where it actually narrows a gap.

policy.notes: Targets a narrow 16-of-26 arXiv concentration in materials science. Sixteen of 20 live entries were Original Research, covering concrete composites, nanoparticles, metastructures and corrosion; reviews, the perspective and editorial remain other. It is one Frontiers origin, added for specialist depth rather than nominal diversity.

The only chemistry source that survived testing. Ten of ten feed entries are wet-lab organic chemistry — synthesis, natural-product isolation, supramolecular assembly — not the computational-method papers that disqualified arXiv physics.chem-ph. Articles resolve end to end at 2093-8090 words, clearing the technical walkthrough's 2000-word floor. Open access, CC BY, robots permits the feed and articles. Narrow by design: organic chemistry only. Every other route failed — ChemRxiv and RSC Advances sit behind Cloudflare and ChemRxiv's robots disallows /rss, Chemistry World returns an AWS WAF challenge, Nature Chemistry is paywalled, and PLOS ONE's chemistry subject feed is 15-20% chemistry and the rest biomedical.

policy.notes: KEPT, and the flag flipped to true to match what the pipeline has always done. The premise that Nature yields full text for 0 of 136 items is wrong: 42 of 136 are full_text_status ok, twelve of them real research full text averaging ~9.6k words, every one carrying a recorded cc-by or cc-by-nc-nd licence. Verified again here: s41586-026-10791-2 resolved to 10274 words with sections classified. Nature and arXiv are the only two sources that reach all three rungs, and Nature is the only non-AI one; its published set is exactly the biology, chemistry and physics the corpus lacks. Roughly half of fresh research resolves and the rest is genuinely soft-paywalled.

Articles are written by researchers, which is native explainer material rather than coverage at one remove. No section is perfectly clean: measured entry by entry, us/health is 48% scientific, us/technology 52% and overlapping AI, us/environment 36%, and us/business 4%. Education was added specifically to counter a 12-of-17 Frontiers concentration; its current titles cover screen use, reading, anxiety, play and classroom heat alongside policy commentary. The development classifier must establish its actual yield, and non-science still stops after one packet call.

~9.6 items a day across genetics, palaeontology, marine biology, particle physics and astronomy — the widest subject spread of any journalism source tested. Four of four resolved as fulltext at 684-730 words, all clearing MIN_WORDS_EXPLAIN. Robots disallows only wp-admin and query strings and names no AI crawlers at all, which is rarer than it should be. Feed links carry utm_ parameters that robots disallows as query strings; strip them before fetching. No feed image.

Broad, general-audience science and health reporting. Its official feed currently carries ten items; two representative articles resolved end to end at 428 and 1,489 words, both with declared images. The recurring multi-topic Short Wave roundup is excluded because one story cannot faithfully represent several unrelated developments; obituaries and policy-adjacent pieces still have to clear the development classifier.

Fast, internationally oriented science news. Two representative reports resolved at 706 and 767 words with images. The live 27-item feed also contained nine audio/video entries, four opinion pieces, an obituary and four puzzle posts; those mechanically identifiable formats are excluded so the classifier sees the actual reporting rather than predictable noise.

Accessible, image-rich features across space, ecology, evolution, archaeology and earth science. All three representative articles resolved as full text at 1,282-1,830 words and all three supplied a page image. The current twelve-item feed was uniformly substantive enough for Glance and usually Explain, without the product-review or multimedia noise seen in other broad candidates.

AGU's earth-science outlet, CC BY-NC-ND 3.0 US, ~3.8 items a day, and the best fix for the missing earth science. Every one of 15 entries syndicates an image — the best image coverage of anything tested, and feed cards need it. Robots disallows nothing, crawl-delay 10. Retrieved at 987 and 746 words. The /research-spotlights/ path is a ~300-word format that resolves as kind=abstract and can never carry an Explain, so it is excluded; /articles/ and /research-and-developments/ carry real body text.

AAS journal highlights that strengthen sparse astronomy coverage. Its unusually large feed returns 600 entries spanning 501 days, so only the publisher-ordered newest 40 are considered; DOI-only entries point to papers rather than AAS Nova articles, while Featured Image posts yielded only 185-256 words, so both formats are excluded. The remaining 16 articles all retrieved as full text with a usable page image; median length is 638 words.

APS's editorial physics publication adds readable coverage beyond raw preprints. The official feed holds 100 entries over roughly three months, so only the newest 30 are considered. Three of three representative entries resolved through their DOI links to full APS Physics articles at 470-1,006 words, each with a declared page image.

Authoritative public-health reports, added to reduce dependence on medicine preprints. The legacy-looking official URL redirects to an active feed with 2,308 entries going back to 2019, so only the newest 30 are considered. Three of three representative downloader links resolved to current CDC reports and extracted 2,204-2,399 words. Reports generally have no suitable preview image, and occasional QuickStats or errata are left for the science classifier to withhold.

0.8 items a day spanning astrophysics, chemistry, brain, climate, ecology, evolution, quantum physics, medicine and human history — the broadest single institutional feed found. Every entry carries an image enclosure. Robots has no Disallow and no crawl-delay. Five of five retrieved as article_html at 682-901 words. Roughly 20% of entries are awards, grants and research-policy announcements; the URL slugs are numeric ids so exclude_patterns cannot filter them and the classifier has to withhold them.

Readable institutional coverage of tissue engineering, implants, bioprinting, biomaterials and biomanufacturing. The feed exposes 50 entries, so the newest 20 are considered; syndicated 'MIT in the media' links are excluded. Three representative research stories retrieved at 1,101-1,506 words and all three declared a usable page image. First-party for MIT research, so it never counts as independent confirmation.

A non-Frontiers counterweight for linguistics, which reached volume almost entirely through one specialist publisher. The live 45-item feed begins with administrative noise but also carries substantive pieces such as 'Separating logic and language' and 'Language development in the brain'; only the newest 20 are considered and the development classifier must earn the source's yield. MIT remains one origin across all topical feeds.

A measured attempt to dilute mathematics' arXiv concentration. The 50-item live feed mixes awards and funding with research; the newest 20 are admitted only to the classifier, not automatically published. This is one MIT origin, not a second independent source beside the language and bioengineering feeds.

0.7 items a day of genuinely explanatory molecular and cell biology plus tool releases. Four of four retrieved at 756-1510 words. Robots allows all bar /static/ and jobs pages, no crawl-delay. Announcement noise is separable by URL path, unlike Max Planck: events sit under /news/connections/ and staff profiles under /news/people-perspectives/, both excluded. No per-category feed exists and no feed image.

CC BY 4.0, explicitly stated at /public/outreach/copyright/. Only ~0.1 items a day, about two releases a month, but the richest institutional text of anything tested: three of three retrieved at 1866, 1987 and 2643 words, pure result-and-explanation astronomy with no puffery, and every entry carries an image. Use this native URL, not the FeedBurner mirror the site advertises and not /public/rss/news/ which is 404. The Announcements feed was tested separately and rejected: it is ministerial visits and annual reports.

The only particle-physics primary source that both parses and retrieves. ~0.2 items a day; three of three retrieved at 466-877 words. Use the category feed, not home.cern/feed/, which is 5 a day of staff bulletins about canteen seating and administrative circulars with no category path to filter on. Even here 2 of 10 entries are obituaries and one is a Courier table of contents, so expect the classifier to withhold roughly a third.

Highest quality per item in the corpus and the most under-used: 4 of 5 hydrated items are fulltext averaging 5136 words, max 11806, and its gate reasons read as successes awaiting publication rather than rejections. Shows 0 published only because just 6 items have ever been ingested. Flag flipped to true — it was false while the pipeline extracted anyway. Every entry syndicates an image. Only weakness is ~5 items a fetch.

Independent explanatory mathematics from the University of Cambridge's Millennium Mathematics Project. Added to reduce an 11-of-15 arXiv concentration, not merely increase volume. Four of four live samples resolved at 456-2,158 words with declared images; the feed mixes current research explanations with evergreen mathematical background and occasional event posts, which the classifier separates.

English-language mathematics coverage from France's national research agency, added after Plus and MIT still left arXiv at 65%. The live feed carries ten articles; three of three samples resolved at 1,240-1,496 words with declared images. It mixes research explanation, profiles and mathematical culture, so the classifier—not the topic page—decides what publishes.

A small, authoritative linguistics archive from France's national research agency. The official topic page exposes six English-language articles on sign languages, rare-language archives, click languages and linguistic communication. It shares the CNRS publishing origin with the mathematics feed, but independently balances the linguistics field away from a single journal publisher.

KEPT ON PROBATION. Retrieval is intermittent: 12 of 20 attempted came back not_found with errors like 'too short (31 words)' on perfectly ordinary /article/ URLs, so the site is sometimes serving an interstitial. The 8 that succeed average ~650 words, barely at the gate, and none has section structure. Its real value is as corroboration for a Nature or arXiv paper, which requires clustering that does not exist yet. Re-audit once clustering lands; if it still shows 0 published, retire it.

Specialist reporting from the Archaeological Institute of America. The feed carries ten current discoveries; three of three samples resolved at 219-358 words with declared images. This is deliberately Glance-oriented reporting, not a source for technical reconstructions that its short articles cannot support.

Independent trade reporting for the otherwise almost empty spaceflight field. The live feed carried 24 entries. Two of two samples resolved at 412 and 939 words with declared images; business-only items still have to clear the development classifier.

Specialist nonprofit reporting and explanation about Solar System science and exploration. The current articles page includes substantive asteroid, Mars, planetary-mission and impact-risk coverage alongside policy and member updates; a 15-item cap and the development classifier keep the latter from padding the feed.
Best published-per-item ratio of any source in the corpus at 3 of 49.
Second best published-per-item ratio at 1 of 17.
First-party lab material; seek paper links and independent coverage.
First-party research blog; attach primary papers when available.
First-party research blog; attach primary papers when available.

Authoritative but first-party. The general news-release feed had published nothing, so two official topical feeds now target Artemis and the space station. A live two-item Artemis test returned one readable 520-word profile and one 104-word image item; the latter is correctly rejected as too short. NASA remains one origin regardless of feed count.
Retired earlier: 1052 items, all blocked, all gated 'no item yielded any text'.

Kept. Resolves to abstracts only — 28 of 60 items, max 449 words — so it can never reach Technical, whose floor is 2000 words. It nonetheless produced 3 of the first 20 published stories with valid Glance and Explain, so the ceiling is real and the source is not useless.

RETIRED. A dead archive: 18 posts across 18 months, newest 2026-07-08, all 18 already hydrated, so there is nothing left for it to deliver. 0 published from 18 items despite 100% retrieval — the worst return of any source that works. First-party GPU marketing that can never validate anything, and the only not_science verdict in the corpus.

RETIRED on three counts. 15 of 20 attempted are paywalled with 'article_html: soft paywall'; the 5 that resolve run 528-835 words with no section structure; and the content is health politics — podcasts, Senate votes, Medicaid injunctions — which the ladder cannot carry as a development or result. 0 published from 40 items. Separately, robots explicitly disallows ClaudeBot, GPTBot and anthropic-ai; our generic UA falls under * only because it is not on their list, and the publisher's intent is unambiguous.

Kept after direct measurement contradicted an image-caption concern: science items reach 1154 words. The new Space Transportation feed targets mission and launcher developments; two of two samples resolved at 970 and 982 words with declared images. Both feeds remain the same first-party ESA origin.
